items.text: C – Cyst or tumour causing airway compression.

rows: Subglottic stenosis, foreign body, severe laryngeal obstruction

items.text: Inspiratory stridor suggests extrathoracic airway obstruction.
Biphasic stridor suggests fixed upper airway obstruction.
Barking cough and hoarseness suggest croup.
Drooling, dysphagia, fever and toxic appearance suggest epiglottitis or another serious upper airway infection.

blocks.text: A child with stridor at rest, severe recession, exhaustion, drooling or reduced consciousness requires urgent airway assessment. Avoid unnecessary examination or agitation if epiglottitis is suspected.

items.text: Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (usually in older children with underlying asthma or cystic fibrosis).

rows: Recurrent, variable wheeze, often with triggers
First episode of wheeze in an infant, usually following an upper respiratory infection
Sudden onset, choking episode, unilateral wheeze
Monophonic wheeze, often worse during expiration
Wheeze may accompany tachypnoea, hepatomegaly and poor feeding

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: A sudden onset of unilateral wheeze in a previously healthy child should raise suspicion of an inhaled foreign body.

rows: Defects in humoral or cellular immunity
Congenital lung malformations and airway defects

items.text: A – Aspiration due to swallowing dysfunction.
E – Enlarged lymph nodes or masses compressing airways.

blocks.title: Recurrent pneumonia is conventionally defined as:

items.text: Two or more episodes in one year, or
Recurrent pneumonia in the same lobe: suspect local obstruction, foreign body, congenital abnormality or extrinsic compression.
Recurrent pneumonia in different lobes: suspect systemic problems such as immunodeficiency, aspiration or cystic fibrosis.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: Always ask about choking episodes, feeding difficulties, recurrent diarrhoea, poor weight gain, family history and HIV exposure where clinically appropriate.

rows: Cystic fibrosis, primary ciliary dyskinesia, airway malformations

items.text: Congenital heart disease with pulmonary congestion.
S – Sudden onset suggesting foreign body.

blocks.text: Other warning features include persistent fever, hypoxaemia and abnormal chest radiographs.
Clinical pearl: A chronic wet cough in a child should prompt consideration of protracted bacterial bronchitis and bronchiectasis rather than automatically being labelled asthma.

subsections.subsection_title: 18.5 Causes of Respiratory Distress in Children

items.text: B – Birth-related causes: prematurity, birth asphyxia.
A – Aspiration: meconium aspiration, milk aspiration.
B – Breathing disorders: pneumonia, bronchiolitis, asthma.
Y – Young infant congenital abnormalities: diaphragmatic hernia, congenital lung malformations.
H – Head bobbing, particularly in infants.
P – Poor feeding and poor respiratory effort in severe disease.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: Respiratory distress describes increased work of breathing. It does not necessarily mean respiratory failure, although it may progress to it.

rows: Low PaO₂, normal or low PaCO₂
Raised PaCO₂, often with low PaO₂

blocks.title: Common reference thresholds in older children are:

items.text: PaCO₂ above 50 mmHg (6.7 kPa) for hypercapnic failure.

blocks.text: These values must be interpreted in the clinical context, especially in neonates and children receiving respiratory support.

OSCE pearl: A child who was initially tachypnoeic and distressed but becomes quieter, exhausted, drowsy or develops poor respiratory effort may be deteriorating. A normalising or rising PaCO₂ in a child with severe asthma is particularly concerning.
Clinical pearl: In children, bronchiectasis is frequently associated with an identifiable underlying disorder. Investigating the cause is as important as treating the infection.

subsections.subsection_title: 18.8 Causes and Risk Factors of Childhood Asthma

items.text: L – Lung infections, especially viral respiratory infections.
A – Allergens, including pollen and animal dander.
Certain medications, such as aspirin or NSAIDs in susceptible individuals.
E – Episodes worse at night or early morning.
Z – Zones of variable airflow obstruction.
E – Evidence of reversibility or variability.

blocks.text: Important diagnostic point: Asthma is characterised by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation. In children old enough to perform reliable testing, spirometry with bronchodilator reversibility testing is useful.
Do not diagnose asthma solely from wheezing in an infant.
An effusion is classified as exudative if at least ONE of the following is present:

items.text: Pleural fluid protein / serum protein greater than 0.5.
Pleural fluid LDH / serum LDH greater than 0.6.
Pleural fluid LDH greater than two-thirds the upper limit of normal serum LDH.

blocks.text: Clinical pearl: In children, pneumonia is a major cause of parapneumonic pleural effusion. Tuberculosis is also an important consideration in high-burden settings, including Nigeria.

rows: Excessive feeding or inappropriate feeding technique

items.text: Food – Milk, food particles and foreign bodies.
Fluid – Saliva, gastric contents and other liquids.
Foreign objects – Toys, nuts, seeds and small objects.
M – Mechanical airway obstruction and atelectasis.
O – Oxygen deprivation and respiratory failure.

blocks.text: OSCE pearl: Recurrent coughing, choking, wet voice or desaturation during feeding should raise suspicion of swallowing dysfunction and aspiration.
